473	
474	        Every relevant slot config key must be truthy. The condition
475	        entity (``CONF_CONDITION``) is truthy when its state is ``on``;
476	        ``off`` is False and any other state (unknown, unavailable,
477	        missing) is None and treated as inactive.
478	        """
479	        slot_config = self._slot_config()
480	        states: dict[str, bool | None] = {}
481	        for key, value in slot_config.items():
482	            if key in (EVENT_CREDENTIAL_USED, CONF_NAME, CONF_PIN, ATTR_IN_SYNC):
483	                continue
484	            if key == CONF_CONDITION:
485	                hass_state = self._hass.states.get(value)
486	                if hass_state is None:
487	                    states[key] = None
488	                elif hass_state.state == STATE_ON:
489	                    states[key] = True
490	                elif hass_state.state == STATE_OFF:
491	                    states[key] = False
492	                else:
493	                    states[key] = None
494	                continue
495	            states[key] = bool(value)
496	
497	        inactive_because_of = [k for k, v in states.items() if not v]
498	        new_active = not inactive_because_of
499	        if (
500	            new_active == self._is_active
501	            and inactive_because_of == self._inactive_because_of
502	        ):
503	            return
504	        self._is_active = new_active
505	        self._inactive_because_of = inactive_because_of
506	        for writer in list(self._active_view_writers):
507	            writer(self._is_active, list(self._inactive_because_of))
508

510	    def _safely_raise_pin_required_issue(self) -> None:
511	        """Create the ``pin_required`` repair issue, logging registry failures."""
512	        try:

515	                DOMAIN,

517	                is_fixable=True,

519	                severity=IssueSeverity.WARNING,
520	                translation_key="pin_required",
521	                translation_placeholders={

523	                    "config_entry_title": self._config_entry.title,

"""Text for lock_code_manager."""

import logging
from typing import override

from homeassistant.components.text import TextEntity, TextMode
from homeassistant.const import CONF_NAME, CONF_PIN
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant, callback
from homeassistant.exceptions import ServiceValidationError
from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er
from homeassistant.helpers.entity_platform import AddEntitiesCallback

from .const import DOMAIN
from .entity import BaseLockCodeManagerEntity
from .ha.entry import LockCodeManagerConfigEntry
from .ha.slot_coordinator import InvalidNameError
from .model.queries import subentry_id_for_slot

_LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)


async def async_setup_entry(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    async_add_entities: AddEntitiesCallback,
) -> bool:
    """Set up config entry."""

    @callback
    def add_standard_text_entities(slot_num: int, ent_reg: er.EntityRegistry) -> None:
        """Add standard text entities for slot."""
        async_add_entities(
            [
                LockCodeManagerText(hass, ent_reg, config_entry, slot_num, *props)
                for props in ((CONF_NAME, TextMode.TEXT), (CONF_PIN, TextMode.PASSWORD))
            ],
            True,
            config_subentry_id=subentry_id_for_slot(config_entry, slot_num),
        )

    config_entry.async_on_unload(
        config_entry.runtime_data.callbacks.register_standard_adder(
            add_standard_text_entities
        )
    )

    return True


class LockCodeManagerText(BaseLockCodeManagerEntity, TextEntity):
    """Text entity for lock code manager."""

    # Defaults for keys with no length constraint (the slot name) and the
    # fallback when bound locks advertise nothing or an unsatisfiable range.
    _DEFAULT_MIN = 0
    _DEFAULT_MAX = 9999

    def __init__(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        ent_reg: er.EntityRegistry,
        config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
        slot_num: int,
        key: str,
        text_mode: TextMode,
    ) -> None:
        """Initialize Text entity."""
        BaseLockCodeManagerEntity.__init__(
            self, hass, ent_reg, config_entry, slot_num, key
        )
        self._attr_mode = text_mode

    @property
    @override
    def native_min(self) -> int:
        """
        Return the minimum value length -- always the permissive default.

        The advertised per-lock minimum is deliberately NOT surfaced here.
        Home Assistant's ``text.set_value`` service rejects
        ``len(value) < native_min`` before the value reaches the coordinator,
        which would block the empty string that clears a slot and would replace
        the coordinator's per-lock error with a generic one. The coordinator
        (``SlotEntityCoordinator._validate_credential_length``) is the
        authoritative minimum gate; an empty PIN is exempt because it clears
        the slot.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MIN

    @property
    @override
    def native_max(self) -> int:
        """
        Return the maximum value length -- always the permissive default.

        The advertised maximum is deliberately NOT surfaced here, for the same
        reason as the minimum. Home Assistant turns ``native_max`` into the
        field's ``maxlength``, so a lock advertising a limit lower than it
        really accepts would stop the keystrokes with no message at all: the
        field simply refuses to grow and nothing says why. The coordinator
        refuses the write instead, naming the lock and the range it claims,
        which is what somebody needs to see to recognise a bad advertisement.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MAX

    @property
    @override
    def native_value(self) -> str | None:
        """Return native value."""
        return self._state

    @override
    async def async_set_value(self, value: str) -> None:
        """Set value of text."""
        coordinator = self._require_slot_coordinator()
        if self.key == CONF_PIN:
            await coordinator.async_request_pin_update(value)
        else:
            try:
                await coordinator.async_request_name_update(value)
            except InvalidNameError as err:
                raise ServiceValidationError(
                    translation_domain=DOMAIN,
                    translation_key=err.error_key,
                    translation_placeholders=err.placeholders,
                ) from err
        self.async_write_ha_state()

    @override
    async def async_added_to_hass(self) -> None:
        """Handle entity added to hass."""
        await BaseLockCodeManagerEntity.async_added_to_hass(self)
        await TextEntity.async_added_to_hass(self)

"""Text for lock_code_manager."""

import logging
from typing import override

from homeassistant.components.text import TextEntity, TextMode
from homeassistant.const import CONF_NAME, CONF_PIN
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant, callback
from homeassistant.exceptions import ServiceValidationError
from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er
from homeassistant.helpers.entity_platform import AddEntitiesCallback

from .const import DOMAIN
from .entity import BaseLockCodeManagerEntity
from .ha.entry import LockCodeManagerConfigEntry
from .ha.slot_coordinator import InvalidNameError
from .model.queries import subentry_id_for_slot

_LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)


async def async_setup_entry(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
    async_add_entities: AddEntitiesCallback,
) -> bool:
    """Set up config entry."""

    @callback
    def add_standard_text_entities(slot_num: int, ent_reg: er.EntityRegistry) -> None:
        """Add standard text entities for slot."""
        async_add_entities(
            [
                LockCodeManagerText(hass, ent_reg, config_entry, slot_num, *props)
                for props in ((CONF_NAME, TextMode.TEXT), (CONF_PIN, TextMode.PASSWORD))
            ],
            True,
            config_subentry_id=subentry_id_for_slot(config_entry, slot_num),
        )

    config_entry.async_on_unload(
        config_entry.runtime_data.callbacks.register_standard_adder(
            add_standard_text_entities
        )
    )

    return True


class LockCodeManagerText(BaseLockCodeManagerEntity, TextEntity):
    """Text entity for lock code manager."""

    # Defaults for keys with no length constraint (the slot name) and the
    # fallback when bound locks advertise nothing or an unsatisfiable range.
    _DEFAULT_MIN = 0
    _DEFAULT_MAX = 9999

    def __init__(
        self,
        hass: HomeAssistant,
        ent_reg: er.EntityRegistry,
        config_entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
        slot_num: int,
        key: str,
        text_mode: TextMode,
    ) -> None:
        """Initialize Text entity."""
        BaseLockCodeManagerEntity.__init__(
            self, hass, ent_reg, config_entry, slot_num, key
        )
        self._attr_mode = text_mode

    @property
    @override
    def native_min(self) -> int:
        """
        Return the minimum value length -- always the permissive default.

        The advertised per-lock minimum is deliberately NOT surfaced here.
        Home Assistant's ``text.set_value`` service rejects
        ``len(value) < native_min`` before the value reaches the coordinator,
        which would block the empty string that clears a slot and would replace
        the coordinator's per-lock error with a generic one. The coordinator
        (``SlotEntityCoordinator._validate_credential_length``) is the
        authoritative minimum gate; an empty PIN is exempt because it clears
        the slot.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MIN

    @property
    @override
    def native_max(self) -> int:
        """
        Return the maximum value length -- always the permissive default.

        The advertised maximum is deliberately NOT surfaced here, for the same
        reason as the minimum. Home Assistant turns ``native_max`` into the
        field's ``maxlength``, so a lock advertising a limit lower than it
        really accepts would stop the keystrokes with no message at all: the
        field simply refuses to grow and nothing says why. The coordinator
        refuses the write instead, naming the lock and the range it claims,
        which is what somebody needs to see to recognise a bad advertisement.
        """
        return self._DEFAULT_MAX

    @property
    @override
    def native_value(self) -> str | None:
        """Return native value."""
        return self._state

    @override
    async def async_set_value(self, value: str) -> None:
        """Set value of text."""
        coordinator = self._require_slot_coordinator()
        if self.key == CONF_PIN:
            await coordinator.async_request_pin_update(value)
        else:
            try:
                await coordinator.async_request_name_update(value)
            except InvalidNameError as err:
                raise ServiceValidationError(
                    translation_domain=DOMAIN,
                    translation_key=err.error_key,
                    translation_placeholders=err.placeholders,
                ) from err
        self.async_write_ha_state()

    @override
    async def async_added_to_hass(self) -> None:
        """Handle entity added to hass."""
        await BaseLockCodeManagerEntity.async_added_to_hass(self)
        await TextEntity.async_added_to_hass(self)

"""
PIN masking for logs, and its reverse for diagnostics.

Logs carry ``pin#xxxxxxxx`` tokens instead of PINs. The deobfuscation
service maps those tokens back using the PINs currently configured.
"""

from collections.abc import Iterable
import re
from typing import Any
import zlib

from homeassistant.config_entries import ConfigEntry
from homeassistant.const import CONF_PIN

from .config import EntryConfig


def mask_pin(
    pin: str | None,
    slot_num: int | str,
    instance_id: str,
) -> str:
    """
    Return a deterministic masked representation of a PIN for logging.

    Uses CRC32 salted with the HA instance ID and slot number so the same
    PIN on the same slot always produces the same 8-char hex token regardless
    of which lock or config entry it belongs to.  Different slots or HA
    instances produce different tokens.
    """
    if not pin:
        return "<empty>"
    salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{pin}"
    return f"pin#{zlib.crc32(salt.encode()) & 0xFFFFFFFF:08x}"


# Token format emitted by ``mask_pin``: literal "pin#" followed by 8 lowercase
# hex chars. Anchored by word boundary on the right so a longer hex string
# isn't truncated and reported as a match.
_PIN_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"pin#[0-9a-f]{8}\b")


def build_pin_deobfuscation_map(
    entries: Iterable[ConfigEntry], instance_id: str
) -> dict[str, str]:
    """
    Build a ``{masked_token: plaintext_pin}`` lookup for every configured PIN.

    Reads each entry's options-or-data view via ``EntryConfig`` so it works
    whether or not the entry has been migrated to options yet. Slots whose
    PIN is empty are skipped because ``mask_pin`` returns ``<empty>`` for
    them and that's not a token we need to reverse.

    Slot is part of the salt, so different ``(slot, pin)`` pairs produce
    different tokens with overwhelming probability — CRC32 has a 32-bit
    output so collisions are mathematically possible but vanishingly
    unlikely at any plausible slot count. The resulting map has one
    entry per configured slot with a PIN.
    """
    table: dict[str, str] = {}
    for entry in entries:
        config = EntryConfig.from_entry(entry)
        for slot_num, slot_config in config.slots.items():
            pin = slot_config.get(CONF_PIN)
            if not pin:
                continue
            table[mask_pin(pin, slot_num, instance_id)] = pin
    return table


def deobfuscate_pins(text: str, table: dict[str, str]) -> tuple[str, dict[str, Any]]:
    """
    Replace ``pin#xxxxxxxx`` tokens in ``text`` using ``table``.

    Tokens not in the table are left verbatim so the output stays
    paste-compatible with the original log (useful when only some PINs
    have been rotated since the log was written). The summary lists the
    distinct unmatched tokens so the caller can see what didn't resolve
    without scanning the text.
    """
    counts = {"total": 0, "matched": 0}
    unmatched: set[str] = set()

    def _replace(match: re.Match[str]) -> str:

    summary: dict[str, Any] = {

        "matched": counts["matched"],
        "unmatched_tokens": sorted(unmatched),
    }
    return deobfuscated, summary

"""Validate a submitted credential against an entry's desired state."""

from dataclasses import dataclass

from homeassistant.const import CONF_CONDITION
from homeassistant.core import callback

from ..const import (
    REASON_CONDITION_NOT_MET,
    REASON_PRECEDENCE,
    REASON_UNKNOWN_CODE,
    REASON_USER_DISABLED,
)
from ..model.queries import get_entry_config
from .entry import LockCodeManagerConfigEntry
from .slot_coordinator import SlotEntityCoordinator


@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)
class ValidationResult:
    """
    Outcome of validating one submitted credential.

    ``user`` is set exactly when ``valid`` is True, and ``reason`` exactly
    when it is False. The slot number the credential sits on is deliberately
    absent: it is internal bookkeeping, and the use is announced by the
    user's name so that no consumer ends up keyed on a number.
    """

    valid: bool
    user: str | None
    reason: str | None


def _failure_reason(matches: list[SlotEntityCoordinator]) -> str:

289	    invalid one announces nothing at all -- the response is the whole answer,

291	    response rather than from an event anyone else could see.

301	    # rather than ``valid`` is also what tells the type checker it is there.

304	        # entity reads this off the bus and records every use it names, so
305	        # nothing here has to know what a target is or whether Lock Code
306	        # Manager manages it.
307	        #

309	        # looks them up in a registry, or reads their state: a code source's
310	        # state can be the cleartext credential that was just typed.
311	        async_fire_credential_used(
312	            hass,
313	            config_entry,

318	            credential_type=CredentialType.PIN,

320	            # actuates, so claiming an unlock would state a fact nobody saw;
321	            # a caller that later needs to say gets a parameter for it.
322	            operation=CredentialOperation.UNKNOWN,

479	async def async_add_users(
480	    hass: HomeAssistant,
481	    users: list[dict[str, Any]],
482	    *,
483	    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
484	    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
485	) -> None:
486	    """
487	    Add one or more users to an entry, numbering them by reading the locks.
488	
489	    All or nothing. Every name is validated, one allocation covers the whole
490	    batch, and one write lands it. Partial success would leave the caller
491	    working out which of a list arrived, and nothing here needs it: every way
492	    this can fail -- a name that means somebody already here, a batch that
493	    will not fit -- is knowable before anything is written.
494	
495	    Adding N users one call at a time would read the locks N times, which on a
496	    battery lock is the difference between usable and not, and would settle
497	    the entry N times over.
498	    """
499	    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
500	    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
501	
502	    additions: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
503	    for entry in users:
504	        name = entry[CONF_NAME]
505	        if error := name_error(name):
506	            raise ServiceValidationError(f"Invalid name {name!r}: {error}")
507	        name = normalize_name(name)
508	        # Checked against the batch as well as the entry: two names in one
509	        # call meaning one person would collapse into a single key on the way
510	        # into storage, taking one of their credentials with it.
511	        if any(
512	            identity(known) == identity(name) for known in (*config.users, *additions)
513	        ):
514	            raise ServiceValidationError(f"A user named {name!r} already exists")
515	
516	        pin = entry.get(CONF_PIN)
517	        enabled = entry.get(CONF_ENABLED, True)
518	        condition = entry.get(CONF_CONDITION)
519	
520	        # The same rule the editor enforces: a slot cannot be programmed
521	        # without something to program.
522	        if enabled and not pin:
523	            raise ServiceValidationError(f"{name!r} cannot be enabled without a PIN")
524	        if condition:
525	            _async_validate_condition(hass, condition)
526	
527	        user: dict[str, Any] = {CONF_ENABLED: enabled}
528	        if pin:
529	            user[CONF_PIN] = pin
530	        if condition:
531	            user[CONF_CONDITION] = condition
532	        additions[name] = user
533	
534	    try:
535	        # One read of the locks for the whole batch, sized to what the entry
536	        # will hold once it lands.
537	        unavailable = await async_allocate_for(
538	            hass,
539	            config_entry,
540	            config.locks,
541	            len(config.users) + len(additions),
542	            # Everyone already here stays, so their numbers need no read.
543	            held=config.assignment.held_by(config.users),
544	        )
545	    except SlotAllocationError as err:
546	        raise ServiceValidationError(
547	            translation_domain=DOMAIN,
548	            translation_key=err.translation_key,
549	            translation_placeholders={
550	                key: str(value) for key, value in err.placeholders.items()
551	            },
552	        ) from err
553	
554	    # Reconciled against the whole set rather than issued directly: everyone
555	    # already here keeps their number by tenure, and only the newcomers are
556	    # given one.
557	    assignment = config.assignment.reconcile(
558	        [*config.users, *additions], start=1, unavailable=unavailable
559	    )
560	    await _async_write_and_settle(
561	        hass,
562	        config_entry,
563	        EntryConfig(
564	            locks=config.locks,
565	            users={**config.users, **additions},
566	            assignment=assignment,
567	            extra=config.extra,
568	        ),
569	    )

589	    is programmed there keeps working. The intent cannot ride in the new
590	    configuration, because the users it concerns are precisely what the new
591	    configuration no longer has, so it is left for the update listener to pick
592	    up as it processes this write.
593	    """
594	    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
595	    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
596	
597	    departing: set[str] = set()
598	    for name in names:
599	        stored = next(
600	            (known for known in config.users if identity(known) == identity(name)),
601	            None,
602	        )
603	        if stored is None:

613

618	    }

"""LCM service-handler implementations."""

import asyncio
import logging
from typing import Any

from homeassistant.config_entries import ConfigEntry
from homeassistant.const import CONF_CONDITION, CONF_ENABLED, CONF_NAME, CONF_PIN
from homeassistant.core import HomeAssistant
from homeassistant.exceptions import HomeAssistantError, ServiceValidationError
from homeassistant.helpers import entity_registry as er

from ..const import (
    ATTR_REASON,
    ATTR_USER,
    ATTR_VALID,
    DOMAIN,
    EXCLUDED_CONDITION_PLATFORMS,
)
from ..model.config import EntryConfig, async_write_entry_config
from ..model.credentials import CredentialType
from ..model.events import (
    CredentialOperation,
    async_fire_credential_used,
)
from ..model.names import identity, name_error, normalize_name
from ..model.queries import get_entry_config, get_loaded_config_entry
from ..sync.registry import SlotTaken
from .allocation import SlotAllocationError, async_allocate_for
from .locks import get_managed_lock
from .runtime import async_write_once
from .slot_coordinator import PinRequiredError, SlotEntityCoordinator
from .validation import validate_credential

_LOGGER = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# How long to wait for the entry to react to a write before returning
# anyway. Generous, because the pass can set up a lock it has never
# spoken to; a caller stuck here is waiting on that, not on this.
_SETTLE_TIMEOUT = 30


async def _async_write_and_settle(
    hass: HomeAssistant, config_entry: ConfigEntry, config: EntryConfig
) -> None:
    """
    Write the entry, and wait for it to have finished reacting.

    ``async_update_entry`` schedules the update listener rather than
    awaiting it, so without this a service returns before the entities for
    the users it changed exist. A script that adds a user and then sets
    their PIN through the new text entity would find nothing to set.

    Waiting on the entry's settle event rather than on the specific
    entities keeps this honest about what it can promise: another write
    landing at the same time can release the wait early. That is no worse
    than not waiting, which is the alternative.
    """
    runtime_data = config_entry.runtime_data
    runtime_data.settled.clear()
    if not async_write_entry_config(hass, config_entry, config):
        # Nothing changed, so no listener will run and nothing will set the
        # event. Waiting here would burn the whole timeout for no reason.
        return
    try:
        async with asyncio.timeout(_SETTLE_TIMEOUT):
            await runtime_data.settled.wait()
    except TimeoutError:
        # The write itself is durable, so this is not a failure to report to
        # the caller -- the entities will appear when the pass finishes.
        _LOGGER.warning(
            "%s (%s): entry did not finish updating within %ss; entities for "
            "this change may appear late",
            config_entry.entry_id,
            config_entry.title,
            _SETTLE_TIMEOUT,
        )


async def async_set_usercode(
    hass: HomeAssistant, lock_entity_id: str, code_slot: int, usercode: str
) -> None:
    """Put a code in a slot no entry manages, through the lock's worker."""
    usercode = usercode.strip()
    if not usercode:
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            "Usercode must not be empty; use the clear operation instead"
        )
    await _async_write_unmanaged(hass, lock_entity_id, code_slot, usercode)


async def async_clear_usercode(
    hass: HomeAssistant, lock_entity_id: str, code_slot: int
) -> None:
    """Clear a slot no entry manages, through the lock's worker."""
    await _async_write_unmanaged(hass, lock_entity_id, code_slot, None)


async def _async_write_unmanaged(
    hass: HomeAssistant, lock_entity_id: str, code_slot: int, usercode: str | None
) -> None:
    """
    Write a slot no entry manages, once, and wait for it.

    A lock that is not answering keeps the write and makes it when it is
    back; one that refuses it, or will not take it after its tries, fails.
    """
    get_managed_lock(hass, lock_entity_id)  # a lock this integration manages
    try:
        done = await async_write_once(hass, lock_entity_id, code_slot, usercode)
    except SlotTaken as err:
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Slot {code_slot} on {lock_entity_id} is managed by an entry; "
            "change it there"
        ) from err
    if done is False:
        raise HomeAssistantError(
            f"{lock_entity_id} did not take the change to slot {code_slot}"
        )


def _stored_user(config: EntryConfig, name: str) -> str:
    """
    Return the name an entry stores for the person ``name`` names.

    Matched the way a user is recognized everywhere else -- whitespace
    normalized and casefolded -- so a caller may spell the name the way they
    say it rather than the way it was stored.
    """
    stored = next(
        (known for known in config.users if identity(known) == identity(name)), None
    )
    if stored is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"No user named {name!r} in this config entry")
    return stored


def _slot_for_user(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None,
    config_entry_title: str | None,
) -> tuple[ConfigEntry, int]:
    """Return the entry and the slot number the named user occupies."""
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
    stored = _stored_user(config, name)
    if (slot_num := config.assignment.slot(stored)) is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"{stored!r} holds no slot in this config entry")
    return config_entry, slot_num


def _slot_coordinator_for(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    config_entry_id: str | None,
    config_entry_title: str | None,
) -> SlotEntityCoordinator:
    """Return the coordinator for the slot the named user occupies."""
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
    stored = _stored_user(config, name)

    # One condition for two ways to hold nothing: a user with no number was
    # never placed, and a number with no coordinator is an entry whose slots
    # and configuration disagree. Both mean there is no slot here to write to
    # or clear, and neither is worth telling apart in the message.
    slot_num = config.assignment.slot(stored)
    coordinators = config_entry.runtime_data.slot_coordinators
    if slot_num is None or (coordinator := coordinators.get(slot_num)) is None:
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"{stored!r} holds no slot in this config entry")
    return coordinator


def _managed_credential_type(credential_type: str) -> CredentialType:
    """
    Return the credential type, refusing kinds this integration cannot store.

    name: str,
    *,
    credential_type: str,
    value: str,

    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,

    Set one of a user's credentials, and let the sync carry it to the locks.

    Addresses the user rather than a lock and a slot number. What that buys
    over ``set_usercode`` is that the credential ends up in the
    configuration: a code written straight to a device is one Lock Code
    Manager does not know about, which the sync may clear back out, and which
    cannot reach a member holding its credentials here rather than on a
    device.

    Routed through the slot's coordinator rather than written to the entry,
    because that is the authoritative gate for a credential write -- it strips
    whitespace and validates the length against every bound lock. Writing the
    configuration directly here would be a second path that skips both.

    inverse of :func:`async_clear_credential` rather than half of it: clearing
    a credential disables the user, so setting one on somebody cleared earlier
    would otherwise leave a code that is present and inert. Off by default,
    because giving a user a credential and letting them in are different
    decisions and only the caller knows whether they are making both.

    refuses a user with no credential and clears the repair issue raised when
    that happened -- and the second call is what runs them.

    # one character, so an empty value never reaches this. Repeating that gate
    # would be a branch nothing can take.

    await coordinator.async_request_pin_update(value)

        # the entry's cached config before returning, so the PIN this checks
        # for is the one just set.
        await coordinator.async_request_active_toggle(True)

    *,

    caller says what was entered and where, and this answers the same
    question the entry's own dashboard would while recording the use.

    A valid code announces itself on the unified credential-used event. An
    invalid one announces nothing at all -- the response is the whole answer,
    so an automation that wants to react to a rejection does so from the
    response rather than from an event anyone else could see.

    what a code is checked against, and a code that no lock has ever been
    programmed with still has an answer here.

    # rather than ``valid`` is also what tells the type checker it is there.

        # entity reads this off the bus and records every use it names, so
        # nothing here has to know what a target is or whether Lock Code
        # Manager manages it.

        # looks them up in a registry, or reads their state: a code source's
        # state can be the cleartext credential that was just typed.

            config_entry,
            name=result.user,
            source=source,
            target=target,

        raise ServiceValidationError(f"Entity {condition} not found")

            f"Entities from the '{entity_entry.platform}' integration are not "

    entity_id: str,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:

    Attach a condition entity to a user.

    A condition gates a person -- their credential works while it is on --
    so the person is what this names. ``set_slot_condition`` named the slot
    number instead, which is internal bookkeeping: an automation holding one
    goes on addressing that number after somebody else comes to occupy it.

        hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title
    )

        slot_num, CONF_CONDITION, entity_id

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:

    Detach a user's condition entity, leaving their credential ungated.

    Removing the gate does not disable anybody: a user with no condition is
    one whose credential simply always applies, which is the ordinary case.
    """

        hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title

    new_config = get_entry_config(config_entry).with_slot_field_removed(
        slot_num, CONF_CONDITION

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    slot: int,
    entity_id: str,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Set a condition entity for a slot."""
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)
    if not config.has_slot(slot):
        raise ServiceValidationError(f"Slot {slot} not found in config entry")

    _async_validate_condition(hass, entity_id)

    new_config = config.with_slot_field_set(slot, CONF_CONDITION, entity_id)
    await _async_write_and_settle(hass, config_entry, new_config)

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    slot: int,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Clear the condition entity from a slot."""
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)

        raise ServiceValidationError(f"Slot {slot} not found in config entry")

async def async_enable_user(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Turn a user on, so their credential is written to the entry's locks.

    Refuses a user holding no credential, because enabling one would
    advertise somebody as able to get in while they hold nothing anybody
    could present. That rule lives in the coordinator, which is also what
    clears the repair issue raised the last time it was hit -- so this goes
    through the same path the dashboard switch does rather than writing the
    field itself.
    """
    coordinator = _slot_coordinator_for(hass, name, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    try:
        await coordinator.async_request_active_toggle(True)
    except PinRequiredError as err:

        # rather than as the caller's problem, which is what it is.

    hass: HomeAssistant,
    name: str,
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Turn a user off, and clear their credential from the entry's locks.

    Unconditional, unlike enabling: there is no state a user can be in that
    makes turning them off invalid. Their credential stays in the
    configuration, so enabling them again restores it without anybody
    having to remember what it was.

async def async_add_users(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    users: list[dict[str, Any]],
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
) -> None:
    """
    Add one or more users to an entry, numbering them by reading the locks.

    All or nothing. Every name is validated, one allocation covers the whole
    batch, and one write lands it. Partial success would leave the caller
    working out which of a list arrived, and nothing here needs it: every way
    this can fail -- a name that means somebody already here, a batch that
    will not fit -- is knowable before anything is written.

    Adding N users one call at a time would read the locks N times, which on a
    battery lock is the difference between usable and not, and would settle
    the entry N times over.
    """
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)

    additions: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] = {}
    for entry in users:
        name = entry[CONF_NAME]
        if error := name_error(name):
            raise ServiceValidationError(f"Invalid name {name!r}: {error}")
        name = normalize_name(name)
        # Checked against the batch as well as the entry: two names in one
        # call meaning one person would collapse into a single key on the way
        # into storage, taking one of their credentials with it.
        if any(
            identity(known) == identity(name) for known in (*config.users, *additions)
        ):
            raise ServiceValidationError(f"A user named {name!r} already exists")

        pin = entry.get(CONF_PIN)
        enabled = entry.get(CONF_ENABLED, True)
        condition = entry.get(CONF_CONDITION)

        # The same rule the editor enforces: a slot cannot be programmed
        # without something to program.
        if enabled and not pin:
            raise ServiceValidationError(f"{name!r} cannot be enabled without a PIN")
        if condition:
            _async_validate_condition(hass, condition)

        user: dict[str, Any] = {CONF_ENABLED: enabled}
        if pin:
            user[CONF_PIN] = pin
        if condition:
            user[CONF_CONDITION] = condition
        additions[name] = user

    try:
        # One read of the locks for the whole batch, sized to what the entry
        # will hold once it lands.
        unavailable = await async_allocate_for(
            hass,
            config_entry,
            config.locks,
            len(config.users) + len(additions),
            # Everyone already here stays, so their numbers need no read.
            held=config.assignment.held_by(config.users),
        )
    except SlotAllocationError as err:
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            translation_domain=DOMAIN,
            translation_key=err.translation_key,
            translation_placeholders={
                key: str(value) for key, value in err.placeholders.items()
            },
        ) from err

    # Reconciled against the whole set rather than issued directly: everyone
    # already here keeps their number by tenure, and only the newcomers are
    # given one.
    assignment = config.assignment.reconcile(
        [*config.users, *additions], start=1, unavailable=unavailable
    )
    await _async_write_and_settle(
        hass,
        config_entry,
        EntryConfig(
            locks=config.locks,
            users={**config.users, **additions},
            assignment=assignment,
            extra=config.extra,
        ),
    )


async def async_delete_users(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    names: list[str],
    *,
    config_entry_id: str | None = None,
    config_entry_title: str | None = None,
    clear_credentials: bool = True,
) -> None:
    """
    Remove one or more users from an entry, and by default from the locks.

    All or nothing, and for the same reason as adding: an unknown name is the
    caller's mistake, and reporting it after removing the others would leave
    them working out what happened.

    ``clear_credentials=False`` hands the credentials over rather than
    deleting them: Lock Code Manager stops managing those slots and whatever
    is programmed there keeps working. The intent cannot ride in the new
    configuration, because the users it concerns are precisely what the new
    configuration no longer has, so it is left for the update listener to pick
    up as it processes this write.
    """
    config_entry = get_loaded_config_entry(hass, config_entry_id, config_entry_title)
    config = get_entry_config(config_entry)

    departing: set[str] = set()
    for name in names:
        stored = next(
            (known for known in config.users if identity(known) == identity(name)),
            None,
        )
        if stored is None:
            raise ServiceValidationError(f"No user named {name!r} in this config entry")
        departing.add(stored)

    if not clear_credentials:
        for stored in departing:
            if slot_num := config.assignment.slot(stored):
                config_entry.runtime_data.retained_pairs.update(
                    (lock_entity_id, slot_num) for lock_entity_id in config.locks
                )

    remaining = {
        known: fields
        for known, fields in config.users.items()
        if known not in departing
    }
    # No unavailable set and so no lock read: a departure issues no numbers,
    # and everyone remaining keeps theirs by tenure.
    await _async_write_and_settle(
        hass,
        config_entry,
        EntryConfig(
            locks=config.locks,
            users=remaining,
            assignment=config.assignment.reconcile(remaining, start=1),
            extra=config.extra,
        ),
    )

    entry: ConfigEntry,

    """
    Set what ``slot`` should hold on a lock ``entry`` holds, if it owns the slot.

    ``wants`` is by credential type, for each type the lock takes; a type
    not named is kept clear. A type the lock no longer takes is let go of,

class _AllocatesInProgress:
    """
    Run allocation as a progress task, so a long lock read is visible.

    A lock that answers one index per round trip can take a minute or more
    per lock, and both flows that allocate are interactive (issue #1536). The
    step that takes the submission starts the task and shows progress; Home
    Assistant re-enters the step when the task finishes, the step hands off
    to its ``<step>_allocated`` sibling, and that one either proceeds or
    re-shows the same form with the refusal. A task already finished when it
    starts goes straight to progress-done.
    """

    # Provided by the FlowHandler this is mixed into.
    hass: HomeAssistant
    async_show_progress: Callable[..., Any]
    async_show_progress_done: Callable[..., Any]
    async def async_step_several(
        self, user_input: dict[str, Any] | None = None
    ) -> SubentryFlowResult:
        """
        Add a block of users at once, one subentry each.

        The same shape and the same validator the setup flow's yaml path
        uses, so what a person pastes to set the entry up is what they paste
        to add to it. Adding them one at a time is the same work spread over
        one dialog and one lock read each; here it is one read and one write,
        which on a lock that answers an index per round trip is the
        difference between usable and not, and which settles the entry once
        rather than once per arrival.

        This does not touch anybody already here: a block that names one of
        them is refused rather than merged. Editing and removing stay where
        they were, one user at a time, so there is still exactly one way to
        change a user who exists.
        """
        entry = self._get_entry()
        config = get_entry_config(entry)
        errors: dict[str, str] = {}
        description_placeholders: dict[str, Any] = {}

        if user_input:
            (
                users,
                validation_errors,
                validation_placeholders,
            ) = await _async_validate_users_yaml(
                self.hass,
                entry,
                user_input[CONF_USERS],
                config.locks,
                taken=config.users,
            )
            errors.update(validation_errors)
            description_placeholders.update(validation_placeholders)

            if not errors:
                assert users is not None
                # One allocation for the whole block, sized to what the entry
                # will hold once it lands. Everybody already here keeps their
                # number by tenure and is not read for.
                (
                    unavailable,
                    allocation_errors,
                    allocation_placeholders,
                ) = await _allocate_for(
                    self.hass,
                    entry,
                    config.locks,
                    len(config.users) + len(users),
                    held=config.assignment.held_by(config.users),
                )
                if unavailable is None:
                    errors.update(allocation_errors)
                    description_placeholders.update(allocation_placeholders)
                else:
                    arrived = {**config.users, **users}
                    assignment = config.assignment.reconcile(
                        arrived, start=1, unavailable=unavailable
                    )
                    # Written through the one write path rather than by
                    # completing the flow: a finished subentry flow creates
                    # exactly one subentry, and this creates as many as were
                    # pasted.
                    async_write_entry_config(
                        self.hass,
                        entry,
                        EntryConfig(
                            locks=config.locks,
                            users=arrived,
                            assignment=assignment,
                            extra=config.extra,
                        ),
                    )
                    warning = _cannot_report(
                        self.hass,
                        config.locks,
                        (assignment.slots[identity(name)] for name in users),
                    )
                    return self.async_abort(
                        reason="users_added_cannot_report"
                        if warning
                        else "users_added",
                        description_placeholders={
                            "num_users": str(len(users)),
                            **(warning or {}),
                        },
                    )

        return self.async_show_form(
            step_id="several",
            data_schema=_users_schema(user_input),
            errors=errors,
            description_placeholders=description_placeholders,
        )

content.thinking:
I realize the schema strips values before the handler knows the credential type, but passwords shouldn't be stripped since an all-space value is technically valid—so I need to move stripping into the handler itself, applying it only for PINs and keeping passwords unstripped but still required to be nonempty.

For the config flow form, I'm adding a password field using a text selector, always shown regardless of whether the entry's locks actually support passwords, since capabilities aren't always known at setup time and a stored password still counts as "enabled" per decision 4 even without a matching lock type.

class CredentialType(StrEnum):
    """
    Kind of credential a user presents to a lock.

    Lock Code Manager writes ``PIN`` and ``PASSWORD``
    (``MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES``), but a use is reported as whichever kind
    the lock says was presented: ``PIN``, ``RFID`` or ``FINGERPRINT``
    (Matter, ZHA, Zigbee2MQTT) or ``FACE`` (Matter). ``NFC`` is reserved so a
    future expansion to more kinds is additive. The members map cleanly to
    both the Z-Wave User Credential Command Class and the Matter DoorLock
    cluster credential-type vocabularies. ``PIN`` deliberately serializes to
    the lowercase wire value the providers already send.
    """

    PIN = "pin"
    RFID = "rfid"  # Radio Frequency Identification tag/card.
    FINGERPRINT = "fingerprint"
    FACE = "face"
    PASSWORD = "REDACTED"
    NFC = "nfc"  # Near Field Communication tag.


# The credential types Lock Code Manager itself manages -- the kinds it can
# write to a lock. Each lock keeps the ones its provider writes and the lock
# advertises (``BaseLock.managed_credential_types``).
#
# The single place to change when that stops being true. Do not restate the
# set anywhere else: every site that depends on which types are managed has
# to move together.
#
# Distinct from what a lock can REPORT. A lock may advertise types Lock Code
# Manager cannot write -- an RFID reader on the door is one -- and a use of
# one of those is still a use worth recording.
MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES: frozenset[CredentialType] = frozenset(
    {CredentialType.PIN, CredentialType.PASSWORD}
)


class UserType(StrEnum):
    """
    How a user is constrained on the lock.

    Modeled minimally for now. ``UNRESTRICTED`` matches the Matter and Z-Wave
    "normal" user with no schedule restrictions, which is the only kind Lock
    Code Manager manages today. Additional kinds (for example schedule- or
    duress-restricted users) can be appended without breaking callers.
    """

    How many credentials a user must present to operate the lock.

    ``SINGLE`` means any one credential is sufficient: a user holding a PIN
    and a REDACTED opens the door with either. Multi-credential rules can be
    appended without breaking callers.
    """

content.thinking:
For Z-Wave, I'm thinking the provider can convert byte limits into character limits for its capabilities (dividing max length by two), so the coordinator stays generic and simply compares character counts against length bounds for each type, with Z-Wave reporting password lengths already in characters.

On the error messaging, I want `_validate_credential_length` to use the friendly credential labels rather than the raw enum value so messages read like "Password length..." instead of "PASSWORD length...".

For duplicate detection within an entry, I'm planning for `async_request_credential_update` to compare a new credential against other slots of the same type in that entry's config, using stripped values for PINs, and raising a ServiceValidationError naming the other user (not the value) since names aren't sensitive. In the config flow's `_validate_user_form`, I realize the duplicate-check parameter is typed as a Collection of strings but is actually being passed name-to-fields mappings from both the setup and subentry flows, so I should correct that type to a Mapping instead.

I'm extending duplicate checks to cover PIN and password fields with dedicated error keys, applying the same logic to YAML-based user imports, the add_users service, and the text entity's set_credential path. I'm also reconsidering whether editing a user with a legacy duplicate PIN should be blocked — deciding it's better to only reject duplicates when the submitted value actually changes from what's stored, keeping backward compatibility for unedited users, and I'm defining a helper to check whether a user's fields contain any credential at all.

I'm mapping credential types to their config keys since they align directly with the enum values, simplifying the lookup into a single helper that builds a dict of configured credentials per user. I'm also working out how clearing a credential should only fully disable it if no other credential remains, and how enabling a user without any credential should raise a dedicated error and repair issue.

For cleanup, I'm figuring out that leftover repair issues from the old "pin_required_" naming need to be deleted at entry setup or removal, while deciding whether the repairs flow should still watch for both old and new issue prefixes in case a leftover exists before setup completes.

I'm reworking the config flow validation so disabling a slot without a credential produces a base-level error like "missing_credential_if_enabled" instead of a PIN-specific field error, since credentials can now be PIN or password. I'm also updating the add_users service, switch entity, and text entities to raise or report CredentialRequiredError consistently, and adjusting the set/clear credential service schema to accept either managed credential type.

I need to be careful with whitespace: since the coordinator strips PINs internally, a schema requiring min length 1 on an unstripped value could let a whitespace-only PIN through that then gets stripped to empty and unintentionally clears the credential, so I should add explicit validation in async_set_credential to raise a ServiceValidationError if the stripped PIN is empty. I'm also adding a password field to the add_user schema and services.yaml, and checking how credential_type options are defined there, plus reviewing the mask_credential helper.

For masking, PIN tokens keep their existing "pin#..." format for backward compatibility while passwords get a "pwd#..." salted token, and I need to decide whether to fully rename mask_pin to mask_credential everywhere it's used across provider files or keep mask_pin as a thin PIN-specific wrapper to minimize churn, since the broader rename would touch many files.

I'll keep mask_pin as-is and add a separate mask_credential function that mask_pin can delegate to, only routing password paths through the new credential-aware function — a reasonable deviation from the spec's literal "becomes" wording. I also need to handle diagnostics masking for passwords, the refused-password rule with its disable handler and repair text, and extend DuplicateCodeError to accept a credential_type parameter so the reason message reflects the right type.

For the entity split, I'm leaning toward a single LockCodeManagerCredentialText class parameterized by credential_type rather than separate Pin/Password subclasses, favoring simplicity. I'm also working out the password entity lifecycle — lock_added/lock_removed handlers in text.py, standard adder logic for adding password entities, removal via a uid formatted as "{slot}|password", and tracking which slots currently have password entities so they get backfilled on startup.

I still need to check the websocket subscribe_code_slot usage, update services.yaml for add_user password and set_credential type, review blueprints for PIN-only assumptions, add a password field with validation to the config flow schema, and plan e2e tests covering setting passwords via the text entity, duplicate refusal, and simulated lock rejection of passwords.

With roughly a dozen tasks mapped out, I need more concrete details before writing code: the entity base's state source and removal UID logic, common text test helpers, the services.yaml add_user section, the repairs fix-flow, how slot_coordinators are stored in runtime_data, and the exact config flow string keys for code_slot pin labels. For Z-Wave, I'm thinking the provider can convert byte limits into character limits for its capabilities (dividing max length by two), so the coordinator stays generic and simply compares character counts against length bounds for each type, with Z-Wave reporting password lengths already in characters.

On the error messaging, I want `_validate_credential_length` to use the friendly credential labels rather than the raw enum value so messages read like "Password length..." instead of "PASSWORD length...".

For duplicate detection within an entry, I'm planning for `async_request_credential_update` to compare a new credential against other slots of the same type in that entry's config, using stripped values for PINs, and raising a ServiceValidationError naming the other user (not the value) since names aren't sensitive. In the config flow's `_validate_user_form`, I realize the duplicate-check parameter is typed as a Collection of strings but is actually being passed name-to-fields mappings from both the setup and subentry flows, so I should correct that type to a Mapping instead.

I'm extending duplicate checks to cover PIN and password fields with dedicated error keys, applying the same logic to YAML-based user imports, the add_users service, and the text entity's set_credential path. I'm also reconsidering whether editing a user with a legacy duplicate PIN should be blocked — deciding it's better to only reject duplicates when the submitted value actually changes from what's stored, keeping backward compatibility for unedited users, and I'm defining a helper to check whether a user's fields contain any credential at all.

I'm mapping credential types to their config keys since they align directly with the enum values, simplifying the lookup into a single helper that builds a dict of configured credentials per user. I'm also working out how clearing a credential should only fully disable it if no other credential remains, and how enabling a user without any credential should raise a dedicated error and repair issue.

For cleanup, I'm figuring out that leftover repair issues from the old "pin_required_" naming need to be deleted at entry setup or removal, while deciding whether the repairs flow should still watch for both old and new issue prefixes in case a leftover exists before setup completes.

I'm reworking the config flow validation so disabling a slot without a credential produces a base-level error like "missing_credential_if_enabled" instead of a PIN-specific field error, since credentials can now be PIN or password. I'm also updating the add_users service, switch entity, and text entities to raise or report CredentialRequiredError consistently, and adjusting the set/clear credential service schema to accept either managed credential type.

I need to be careful with whitespace: since the coordinator strips PINs internally, a schema requiring min length 1 on an unstripped value could let a whitespace-only PIN through that then gets stripped to empty and unintentionally clears the credential, so I should add explicit validation in async_set_credential to raise a ServiceValidationError if the stripped PIN is empty. I'm also adding a password field to the add_user schema and services.yaml, and checking how credential_type options are defined there, plus reviewing the mask_credential helper.

For masking, PIN tokens keep their existing "pin#..." format for backward compatibility while passwords get a "pwd#..." salted token, and I need to decide whether to fully rename mask_pin to mask_credential everywhere it's used across provider files or keep mask_pin as a thin PIN-specific wrapper to minimize churn, since the broader rename would touch many files.

I'll keep mask_pin as-is and add a separate mask_credential function that mask_pin can delegate to, only routing password paths through the new credential-aware function — a reasonable deviation from the spec's literal "becomes" wording. I also need to handle diagnostics masking for passwords, the refused-password rule with its disable handler and repair text, and extend DuplicateCodeError to accept a credential_type parameter so the reason message reflects the right type.

For the entity split, I'm leaning toward a single LockCodeManagerCredentialText class parameterized by credential_type rather than separate Pin/Password subclasses, favoring simplicity. I'm also working out the password entity lifecycle — lock_added/lock_removed handlers in text.py, standard adder logic for adding password entities, removal via a uid formatted as "{slot}|password", and tracking which slots currently have password entities so they get backfilled on startup.

I still need to check the websocket subscribe_code_slot usage, update services.yaml for add_user password and set_credential type, review blueprints for PIN-only assumptions, add a password field with validation to the config flow schema, and plan e2e tests covering setting passwords via the text entity, duplicate refusal, and simulated lock rejection of passwords.

def _pin_caps(min_length: int, max_length: int) -> LockCapabilities:

async def test_request_pin_update_rejects_out_of_range_pin(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """A PIN shorter than the lock minimum is rejected and never written."""
    runtime_data = lock_code_manager_config_entry.runtime_data
    for lock in runtime_data.locks.values():
        lock._capabilities_cache = _pin_caps(4, 8)
    coordinator = runtime_data.slot_coordinators[1]

    with pytest.raises(ServiceValidationError):
        await coordinator.async_request_pin_update("12")

    # The rejected PIN must not reach config.
    assert get_entry_config(lock_code_manager_config_entry).slot(1).get(CONF_PIN) == (
        "1234"
    )

async def test_request_pin_update_auto_disables_on_empty(
    hass: HomeAssistant,
    mock_lock_config_entry,
    lock_code_manager_config_entry,
):
    """Clearing the PIN on an enabled slot disables the slot in one write."""
    runtime_data = lock_code_manager_config_entry.runtime_data
    coordinator = runtime_data.slot_coordinators[1]
    assert coordinator.is_enabled is True
    assert coordinator.pin_value == "1234"

    await coordinator.async_request_pin_update("")
    await hass.async_block_till_done()

    config = get_entry_config(lock_code_manager_config_entry).slot(1)
    assert config.get(CONF_PIN) == ""
    assert config.get(CONF_ENABLED) is False
    assert coordinator.is_enabled is False

    state = hass.states.get(SLOT_1_PIN_ENTITY)
    assert state is not None
    assert state.state == ""
    state = hass.states.get(SLOT_1_ENABLED_ENTITY)
    assert state is not None
    assert state.state == STATE_OFF

# Password PR 2b: password in the configuration — Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** A user can hold a password as well as, or instead of, a PIN. It is stored in their configuration, set from a text entity, the config flow and the actions, and Lock Code Manager keeps it in sync on every lock that takes passwords (Virtual only until PR 4).

**Architecture:** The core already keeps one address per (slot, credential type) and wants nothing for a password (PR 2a, #1770). This PR gives the password a configuration field (`password`, beside `pin`), makes the slot coordinator want it, and opens every user-facing write path to it: the text entity, `set_credential`/`clear_credential`/`add_user`, the config flow and the setup YAML. The credential-required rule becomes "at least one credential of any type". A refused value holds only its own credential unless it was the user's only one (spec decision 11). Duplicates are refused at configuration time for both types (decision 12).

**Tech Stack:** Python 3.14, Home Assistant custom integration, voluptuous, pytest + pytest-homeassistant-custom-component, Hypothesis.

**Spec:** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-22-password-credential-design.md` (decisions 4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12; sections "Configuration and the credential-required rule", "Entities and validation", "Services and websocket").
**Carryover:** `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-23-password-pr2-carryover.md`, "For 2b".

---

## Ground rules for every task

- Worktree: `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/password-config` (branch `feat/password-config`, from `origin/main` at `eca7020b`). **Use absolute paths.** Never edit the main checkout.
- Python: `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.venv/bin/python`. Below, `PY` means that path, and `W` means `custom_components/lock_code_manager`.
- Run tests from the worktree root: `cd /Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/password-config && $PY -m pytest <paths> -q -p no:cacheprovider`.
- Before every commit: `prek run --all-files` (ruff, flake8, mypy). Fix what it reports; do not skip hooks.
- Never put a credential value in an error message, a log line, or an exception's `str()`. Every new error names the rule, never the value.
- `strings.json` and `translations/en.json` must stay identical. After editing `strings.json`, run `cp $W/strings.json $W/translations/en.json`.
- Comments state intent, not history. No "previously", no "used to", no review narrative.
- Commit messages: conventional (`feat(config): ...`), end with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
- Tests for a task go in the same commit as its code.
- After each task's tests pass, break the rule on purpose (one mutation per rule named in the task) and confirm a named test fails, then restore. Use a script that restores in `finally`.

## Decisions this plan makes (raise with Raman if any is wrong)

1. **The PIN keeps today's character rules.** The spec's validator says "digits for PIN". This PR adds the password rule only: refusing non-digit PINs would break users whose locks accept them (the User Code CC alphanumeric follow-up in the spec's "Out" list). The validator is shaped so a PIN rule is one line later.
2. **Password length is checked in characters.** `_validate_credential_length` compares `len(value)` against `length_bounds(type)` for every type. Z-Wave's byte limits (spec decision 1) become character limits in the Z-Wave provider's capabilities in PR 4 (`max_length // 2`). Recorded in the carryover file in Task 11.
3. **The config flow shows a Password field only when the entry offers passwords.** In the subentry flows (add a user, edit a user) the field appears when a lock in the entry takes passwords. The setup flow's form has no locks set up yet, so it has no Password field; its YAML path accepts `password:`. Editing a user whose password is stored but not offered keeps it (decision 10).
4. **`mask_pin` stays; `mask_credential` is added.** A PIN's token is unchanged (`pin#…`), so existing logs still deobfuscate. A password's token is `pwd#…`, salted with its type, so a PIN and a password with the same value mask differently.
5. **A refused value's repair** reuses the per-lock `slot_suspended_*` issue id with a new translation key, `credential_refused`, so acknowledging it resumes the credential (the existing `ResumeSlotRepairFlow`).
6. **A duplicate is refused only when the value changes.** Editing a user whose PIN already matches another user's (a configuration saved before this rule) does not fail on the untouched PIN.
7. **The generator and websocket payloads are PR 3** (Raman, 2026-10-24).

```python
# Printable ASCII, space through tilde: what every lock that takes a password
# can be sent, two bytes each on the wire (spec decision 1).
_PASSWORD_CHARACTERS: Final = frozenset(map(chr, range(0x20, 0x7F)))


def credential_value_error(credential_type: CredentialType, value: str) -> str | None:
    """
    Return why ``value`` cannot be a ``credential_type``; None if it can.

    The reason names the rule and never the value: it reaches errors and
    logs. A PIN has no character rule here -- each lock's own applies.
    """
    if (
        credential_type is CredentialType.PASSWORD
        and not set(value) <= _PASSWORD_CHARACTERS
    ):
        return "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces"
    return None
```

```python
from homeassistant.const import CONF_PIN

from .config import EntryConfig
from .credentials import CredentialType

# Token prefix by credential type. A PIN's is what logs have always carried.
_TOKEN_PREFIX = {CredentialType.PIN: "pin", CredentialType.PASSWORD: "pwd"}


def mask_pin(pin: str | None, slot_num: int | str, instance_id: str) -> str:
    """Return the masked form of a PIN for logging (see ``mask_credential``)."""
    return mask_credential(pin, slot_num, instance_id, CredentialType.PIN)


def mask_credential(
    value: str | None,
    slot_num: int | str,
    instance_id: str,
    credential_type: CredentialType,
) -> str:
    """
    Return a deterministic masked representation of a credential for logging.

    CRC32 salted with the HA instance ID and slot number, so the same value
    on the same slot always produces the same 8-char hex token regardless of
    which lock or config entry it belongs to. Any type but the PIN is salted
    with its type too, so a PIN and a password of the same value differ.
    """
    if not value:
        return "<empty>"
    if credential_type is CredentialType.PIN:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{value}"
    else:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{credential_type}:{value}"
    prefix = _TOKEN_PREFIX[credential_type]
    return f"{prefix}#{zlib.crc32(salt.encode()) & 0xFFFFFFFF:08x}"


# Tokens emitted by ``mask_credential``: a type prefix, "#", then 8 lowercase
# hex chars. Anchored by word boundary on the right so a longer hex string
# isn't truncated and reported as a match.
_PIN_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"(?:pin|pwd)#[0-9a-f]{8}\b")
```

```python
    async def async_request_pin_update(self, value: str) -> None:
        """Apply a PIN write (see ``async_request_credential_update``)."""
        await self.async_request_credential_update(CredentialType.PIN, value)

    async def async_request_credential_update(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType, value: str
    ) -> None:
        """
        Apply a credential write requested by a text entity or an action.

        A PIN is stripped: a submitted code is stripped before it is matched,
        so padding kept on the stored side makes a credential nothing typed
        can match. A password is kept as typed (spec decision 7).

        A non-empty value must pass the type's character rule and every bound
        lock's length range; an empty one clears the credential and is
        exempt. This is the authoritative gate: the text entity keeps
        ``native_min`` and ``native_max`` permissive so Home Assistant's
        ``text.set_value`` neither rejects the empty clear nor pre-empts the
        per-lock error built here -- whose errors would quote the value.

        Clearing the slot's last credential turns an enabled slot off: a user
        with nothing to present would read as active (spec decision 4).
        """
        if credential_type is CredentialType.PIN:
            value = value.strip()
        if value:
            if error := credential_value_error(credential_type, value):
                raise ServiceValidationError(error)
            self._validate_credential_length(value, credential_type)

        updates: dict[str, Any] = {credential_type.value: value}
        remaining = {
            other: held
            for other, held in credential_values(self._slot_config()).items()
            if other is not credential_type
        }
        if not value and not remaining and self.is_enabled:
            _LOGGER.debug(
                "%s: last credential cleared on enabled slot, auto-disabling",
                self._log_prefix,
            )
            updates[CONF_ENABLED] = False

        self._write_config_fields(updates)
```

```python
    def _refuse_duplicate(self, credential_type: CredentialType, value: str) -> None:
        """
        Refuse ``value`` if another user in the entry holds it as the same type.

        Two users sharing a credential: whoever presents it is recorded as
        either, and turning one off leaves it working (spec decision 12).
        Names the other user, never the value.

        config = get_entry_config(self._config_entry)
        other = next(
            (
                slot_config[CONF_NAME]
                for slot_num, slot_config in config.slots.items()
                if slot_num != self._slot_num
                and credential_values(slot_config).get(credential_type) == value
            ),
            None,
        )
        if other is not None:
            label = CREDENTIAL_LABELS[credential_type.value]
```

```python
            CredentialType.PASSWORD in lock.managed_credential_types

                f"Remove slot {slot_num} password entity",

        callbacks.register_standard_adder(add_standard_text_entities)
    )
```

```python
def _managed_credential_type(credential_type: str) -> CredentialType:
    """
    Return the credential type, refusing kinds this integration cannot store.

    Every member of ``CredentialType`` is accepted by the schema so the
    vocabulary is the providers' rather than this action's, and the ones Lock
    Code Manager cannot store are refused here instead -- the caller learns
    that RFID is a real kind it does not store, rather than that the word is
    invalid.
    """
    kind = CredentialType(credential_type)
    if kind not in MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES:
        supported = ", ".join(sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES))
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Lock Code Manager cannot store a {kind} credential. "
            f"Supported: {supported}"
        )
    return kind
```

```python
# Printable ASCII, space through tilde: what every lock that takes a password
# can be sent, two bytes each on the wire (spec decision 1).
_PASSWORD_CHARACTERS: Final = frozenset(map(chr, range(0x20, 0x7F)))


def credential_value_error(credential_type: CredentialType, value: str) -> str | None:
    """
    Return why ``value`` cannot be a ``credential_type``; None if it can.

    The reason names the rule and never the value: it reaches errors and
    logs. A PIN has no character rule here -- each lock's own applies.
    """
    if (
        credential_type is CredentialType.PASSWORD
        and not set(value) <= _PASSWORD_CHARACTERS
    ):
        return "Password may only contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces"
    return None
```

```python
from homeassistant.const import CONF_PIN

from .config import EntryConfig
from .credentials import CredentialType

# Token prefix by credential type. A PIN's is what logs have always carried.
_TOKEN_PREFIX = {CredentialType.PIN: "pin", CredentialType.PASSWORD: "pwd"}


def mask_pin(pin: str | None, slot_num: int | str, instance_id: str) -> str:
    """Return the masked form of a PIN for logging (see ``mask_credential``)."""
    return mask_credential(pin, slot_num, instance_id, CredentialType.PIN)


def mask_credential(
    value: str | None,
    slot_num: int | str,
    instance_id: str,
    credential_type: CredentialType,
) -> str:
    """
    Return a deterministic masked representation of a credential for logging.

    CRC32 salted with the HA instance ID and slot number, so the same value
    on the same slot always produces the same 8-char hex token regardless of
    which lock or config entry it belongs to. Any type but the PIN is salted
    with its type too, so a PIN and a password of the same value differ.
    """
    if not value:
        return "<empty>"
    if credential_type is CredentialType.PIN:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{value}"
    else:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{credential_type}:{value}"
    prefix = _TOKEN_PREFIX[credential_type]
    return f"{prefix}#{zlib.crc32(salt.encode()) & 0xFFFFFFFF:08x}"


# Tokens emitted by ``mask_credential``: a type prefix, "#", then 8 lowercase
# hex chars. Anchored by word boundary on the right so a longer hex string
# isn't truncated and reported as a match.
_PIN_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"(?:pin|pwd)#[0-9a-f]{8}\b")
```

```python
def available_credential_types(
    entry: LockCodeManagerConfigEntry,
) -> frozenset[CredentialType]:

    return frozenset({CredentialType.PIN}).union(
```

```python
        """Apply a PIN write (see ``async_request_credential_update``)."""
        await self.async_request_credential_update(CredentialType.PIN, value)

    async def async_request_credential_update(
        self, credential_type: CredentialType, value: str
    ) -> None:
        """
        Apply a credential write requested by a text entity or an action.

        A PIN is stripped: a submitted code is stripped before it is matched,
        so padding kept on the stored side makes a credential nothing typed
        can match. A password is kept as typed (spec decision 7).

        A non-empty value must pass the type's character rule and every bound
        lock's length range; an empty one clears the credential and is
        exempt. This is the authoritative gate: the text entity keeps
        ``native_min`` and ``native_max`` permissive so Home Assistant's
        ``text.set_value`` neither rejects the empty clear nor pre-empts the
        per-lock error built here -- whose errors would quote the value.

        Clearing the slot's last credential turns an enabled slot off: a user
        with nothing to present would read as active (spec decision 4).
        """
        if credential_type is CredentialType.PIN:
            value = value.strip()
        if value:
            if error := credential_value_error(credential_type, value):
                raise ServiceValidationError(error)
            self._validate_credential_length(value, credential_type)

        updates: dict[str, Any] = {credential_type.value: value}
        remaining = {
            other: held
            for other, held in credential_values(self._slot_config()).items()
            if other is not credential_type
        }
        if not value and not remaining and self.is_enabled:
            _LOGGER.debug(
                "%s: last credential cleared on enabled slot, auto-disabling",
                self._log_prefix,
            )
            updates[CONF_ENABLED] = False

        self._write_config_fields(updates)
```

```python
    def _refuse_duplicate(self, credential_type: CredentialType, value: str) -> None:
        """
        Refuse ``value`` if another user in the entry holds it as the same type.

        Two users sharing a credential: whoever presents it is recorded as
        either, and turning one off leaves it working (spec decision 12).

                if slot_num != self._slot_num
                and credential_values(slot_config).get(credential_type) == value
            ),
            None,
```

```python
def _managed_credential_type(credential_type: str) -> CredentialType:
    """
    Return the credential type, refusing kinds this integration cannot store.

    Every member of ``CredentialType`` is accepted by the schema so the
    vocabulary is the providers' rather than this action's, and the ones Lock
    Code Manager cannot store are refused here instead -- the caller learns
    that RFID is a real kind it does not store, rather than that the word is
    invalid.
    """
    kind = CredentialType(credential_type)
    if kind not in MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES:
        supported = ", ".join(sorted(MANAGED_CREDENTIAL_TYPES))
        raise ServiceValidationError(
            f"Lock Code Manager cannot store a {kind} credential. "
            f"Supported: {supported}"
        )
    return kind
```

```python
from homeassistant.const import CONF_PIN

from .config import EntryConfig
from .credentials import CredentialType

# Token prefix by credential type. A PIN's is what logs have always carried.
_TOKEN_PREFIX = {CredentialType.PIN: "pin", CredentialType.PASSWORD: "pwd"}


def mask_pin(pin: str | None, slot_num: int | str, instance_id: str) -> str:
    """Return the masked form of a PIN for logging (see ``mask_credential``)."""
    return mask_credential(pin, slot_num, instance_id, CredentialType.PIN)


def mask_credential(
    value: str | None,
    slot_num: int | str,
    instance_id: str,
    credential_type: CredentialType,
) -> str:
    """
    Return a deterministic masked representation of a credential for logging.

    CRC32 salted with the HA instance ID and slot number, so the same value
    on the same slot always produces the same 8-char hex token regardless of
    which lock or config entry it belongs to. Any type but the PIN is salted
    with its type too, so a PIN and a password of the same value differ.
    """
    if not value:
        return "<empty>"
    if credential_type is CredentialType.PIN:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{value}"
    else:
        salt = f"{instance_id}:{slot_num}:{credential_type}:{value}"
    prefix = _TOKEN_PREFIX[credential_type]
    return f"{prefix}#{zlib.crc32(salt.encode()) & 0xFFFFFFFF:08x}"


# Tokens emitted by ``mask_credential``: a type prefix, "#", then 8 lowercase
# hex chars. Anchored by word boundary on the right so a longer hex string
# isn't truncated and reported as a match.
_PIN_TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"(?:pin|pwd)#[0-9a-f]{8}\b")
```

```python
            if other is not credential_type
```

```python
    def _refuse_duplicate(self, credential_type: CredentialType, value: str) -> None:
        """
        Refuse ``value`` if another user in the entry holds it as the same type.
```

```python
from .ha.slot_coordinator import InvalidNameError
```
